articles.title: Ohio construction workers found a kitten trapped inside an excavator; now she has her own hard hat and a job working with them
articles.summary: US News: A routine day at a construction site in Barberton, Ohio, turned into an unexpected animal rescue when workers discovered a tiny kitten trapped inside .
articles.body: A routine day at a construction site in Barberton, Ohio, turned into an unexpected animal rescue when workers discovered a tiny kitten trapped inside an excavator. The crew at River Reach Construction heard persistent meowing coming from a Komatsu machine and soon realised that the cries were coming from somewhere inside the heavy equipment. Supervisor Chase Guello investigated and helped free the kitten after removing the excavatorâs skid plate. The tiny rescue was later named Sue and quickly became part of the construction crewâs story. What makes the tale even more adorable is what happened next. Sue was given a tiny high-visibility vest and a miniature hard hat, transforming the rescued kitten into the construction companyâs unofficial mascot.Ohio construction workers find kitten trapped inside an excavatorThe unusual rescue began when workers at River Reach Construction heard a kitten crying from inside one of their excavators. The sound was coming from somewhere within the heavy machinery rather than from around the construction site, prompting supervisor Chase Guello to investigate. He eventually discovered the tiny kitten hiding inside the Komatsu excavator. Workers carefully removed the machineâs skid plate, allowing them to reach the animal and get her out safely. The rescue was filmed and later shared online, where the sight of a tiny kitten emerging from a huge piece of construction equipment quickly captured peopleâs attention. For the workers, however, the priority was simply getting the frightened animal out of the machinery without hurting her.The tiny kitten was named Sue after the rescueOnce the kitten was safely out of the excavator, the workers gave her the name Sue as a playful reference to the Komatsu machine in which she had been found. The crew could not locate her mother following the rescue, so Sue was placed with a foster family where she could receive care while recovering. Although she was no longer living inside the construction machinery, the workers who rescued her continued to follow her progress. What started as an unexpected discovery at a worksite soon developed into a much more heartwarming story, with the crew becoming attached to the tiny kitten they had pulled from the excavator.Sue is set to become the construction companyâs shop catSueâs connection with the construction crew did not end with her rescue. River Reach Construction decided to keep her as part of the companyâs extended family, with plans for her to become the shop cat. Local reporting said she will be cared for by shop mechanic Jared and his family. That means the kitten has effectively gone from an unexpected stowaway inside a piece of heavy machinery to a permanent member of the construction companyâs world. While calling her a worker is clearly playful, Sue now has something resembling an official role at the company, giving the tiny rescue an unusually happy ending.The rescued kitten even received her own hard hatSueâs new status came with some remarkably appropriate accessories. Following the attention generated by her rescue, the kitten received a miniature high-visibility vest and a tiny hard hat. The hard hat was made with openings that allow her ears to fit through, making the little construction outfit even more adorable. Photos of Sue wearing the gear helped turn her into the perfect mascot for a construction company. She may not be capable of operating an excavator or carrying out actual construction work, but she certainly looks the part of the crewâs smallest member.Her rescue story quickly captured attention onlineRiver Reach Construction shared footage and updates about Sue on social media, helping the unusual rescue reach audiences far beyond the Ohio construction site. Viewers were particularly drawn to the contrast between the enormous excavator and the tiny kitten that had somehow ended up inside it. The story also prompted plenty of playful reactions, with people online joking about Sue receiving her own hard hat and effectively becoming the crewâs newest employee. The attention has given the construction workersâ unexpected rescue a life far beyond the original incident and turned Sue into a memorable internet mascot.From excavator stowaway to construction mascotSueâs journey is remarkable because of how quickly her circumstances changed. She went from being a vulnerable kitten trapped inside heavy machinery to receiving care from a foster family and eventually finding a permanent place connected to the construction crew that rescued her. Her tiny safety vest and hard hat are clearly more about fun than function, but they perfectly capture the affection the workers have developed for her. What could have ended as a dangerous incident involving an animal trapped inside an excavator instead became a heartwarming rescue story. Now Sue has a safe future, a family to care for her and perhaps the most unusual job title on the construction site, the crewâs tiny shop cat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump
articles.summary: The president is using US dominance to challenge allies and enemies alike - but both Canada and Iran have found ways to fight back.
articles.body:
Two days before US-Canada trade talks dramatically derailed, Vice-President JD Vance was telling an audience at a private fundraiser that Prime Minister Mark Carney was a "very sweet guy".

In a private audio recording leaked to the Canadian Press, Vance reportedly went on to say that Carney "comes in and puffs his chest out and says: 'I'm going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.'"

He described that approach as "hilarious" because the Canadians ultimately "climb down on a lot of issues".

Maybe those comments, which received considerable coverage in Canada, were not the proximate cause for Carney's diplomats to pack up and go home over the weekend. But they certainly didn't help.

Carney's move abruptly terminated negotiations over a new trade agreement and sparked a fresh round of tariffs between neighbours who conduct more than $872bn (£640bn) in bilateral annual trade.

The serious and deepening rift - and Vance's comments - offer the latest example of a Trump administration willing to exert force on the global stage against friend and foe alike, again highlighting the potentially disruptive consequences of such actions.

What's more, if Trump thought the Canadians would cave in the face of American pressure - as many US allies have done over the past 19 months - he may have miscalculated. And the consequences of that mistake could linger for the rest of his presidency.

While the latest rupture is striking, friction between the US and Canada dates back to the first Trump administration and the negotiations that created the USMCA: the deal replacing the 1990s-era North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta).

Complicating matters were personal clashes between Trump and Justin Trudeau, who was then Canada's prime minister. As Trump prepared to return to the White House in late 2024, he derisively referred to Trudeau as "governor" and to Canada as America's "51st State."

Underlying those insults was a geopolitical outlook that positioned the US primarily as a hemispheric power entitled to exert political, military, and economic influence over its immediate region – and that most definitely included Canada.

Administration officials viewed Canada as contributing too little to regional defence while disproportionately benefiting from trade with its southern neighbour.

In Trump's worldview, where economic security and national security are inextricably linked, Canada and Mexico - two of America's largest trading partners - became early, obvious targets.

Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs Published 13 hours ago

Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war Published 1 day ago

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump Published 1 day ago

How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump

It's why the US president said he wanted to take over Greenland too.

"If you listen to really anybody in state, treasury, or commerce [departments], you will hear the phrase 'economic security is national security'," said Drew Delong, head of corporate statecraft at the Kearney Foresight think tank.

By the start of this year, however, as North American trade negotiations proceeded in fits and starts, Trump's attention shifted away from Canada to his military interventions in Venezuela and then the Middle East.

Across every region, though, the core line of Trump's international strategy remains consistent: the US is a dominant power capable of imposing its will for national benefit.

Trump's power tested by Canada - and Iran

But power has limits. Trump's second term has been a continuous test of those limits - and, at times, a lesson in finding exactly where they are.

While obvious differences exist between a shooting war in Iran and a trade dispute with Canada, the lessons are not dissimilar. In both, the US faces a counterpart that, despite having far less overall power, retains the means to retaliate.

For Iran, that leverage lies in targeting US allies and disrupting global commerce by threatening maritime chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz.

Canada, for its part, is beginning to test its own ability to inflict economic pain. Tuesday's targeted tariffs mark a first step. Future measures could include restricting US access to Canadian energy and critical minerals, alongside consumer boycotts of American goods.

"As the broader world shifts into a more economic security theatre, you see this game of chokepoints and leverage angles continue to pan out across supply chains," said DeLong. Countries just have to look for them, he added.

For the moment, clear exit ramps are scarce. Trump has escalated his rhetoric, repeatedly accusing Canada of "ripping off" the US, while Ontario Premier Doug Ford fired back by telling the American president to "kiss my ass".

"Every time we push allies and partners away, I think we incentivise them to look for new relationships and new partnerships rather than trying to acquiesce to US demands," said Imran Bayoumi, deputy director of the GeoStrategy Initiative at the Atlantic Council.

Still, room remains for cooler heads to prevail. Canada's new tariffs take effect in two weeks, while the most significant US retaliation - a 50% tariff on Canadian-built vehicles and auto parts - will not kick in until early 2027.

As with any conflict - economic or military - a cycle of escalation can prove difficult to break. However, the multi-month buffer before the next wave of US tariffs gives negotiators space to restart talks. Until Friday night, these had been showing some progress.

A more pressing deadline is November's US midterm elections. Democratic congressional victories could significantly curtail Trump's authority - or unexpected Republican success could embolden him further.

At present, Ottawa seems content to bet on the former outcome, calculating that fear of a midterm blowout in key industrial battlegrounds like Michigan and Ohio will force Trump to back down before ballots are cast.

"I don't think there's the kind of internal political divisions in Canada that maybe the Trump administration would have expected," Bayoumi said. "I think Carney has a lot of political runway to really get a good deal for Canada and not settle for anything less."

There is another possibility that Carney has aired publicly since Trump returned to office, however.

Canada may continue shifting away from the US altogether, charting a course that deliberately widens the distance between the two nations. As Carney noted: "We cannot depend on traditional alliances when the rules of the game have fundamentally changed."

While geographic proximity ensures the two countries will remain intertwined, the deeply integrated economic relationship of recent decades may be coming to an end.

In that respect, Canada presents a contrast with Mexico, which appears to be opting for even closer economic integration with the US. Meanwhile, other global trading partners - including US allies in Europe and Asia - are watching Canada's "elbows up" resistance as a plausible blueprint for future dealings with Trump.

"Ten years from now, this is going to be taught in classrooms," said DeLong. "You have these bifurcating paths within North America, and the question is: Are they going to come back together, or is this going to continue to split? And if it does, who benefits most in the long run?"

If the supposedly easygoing Canadians can stand up to their pugnacious – and powerful - neighbour, others may decide they can, too.

articles.title: Thameslink to replace over 60,000 'ironing board' train seats
articles.summary: Govia Thameslink Railway says these upgrades are part of the wider renationalisation plans.
articles.body:
More than 60,000 seats on Thameslink trains are set to be upgraded as part of plans announced by Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR), less than 100 days after it came under public ownership.

All 115 Thameslink trains will get new seat cushions and backrests, replacing the much-criticised seats dubbed "ironing boards" by passengers.

The work is expected to begin in 2027 and take place over a two-year period.

First-class seats would also receive upgraded seat cushions, while seat-back tables would be installed on the 70 trains that do not currently have them, GTR added.

The seat upgrades are part of wider improvements planned for the Thameslink network after GTR came into public ownership in May 2026 .

Other measures included an increase in Gatwick Express services from December and a programme to refurbish train toilets and remove graffiti across the fleet.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said: "We'll start getting rid of the dreaded 'ironing board seats' so passengers can enjoy comfier, more pleasant journeys on some of Britain's busiest commuter routes."

Alexander said wider rail reforms would continue under the planned Great British Railways organisation, which is intended to oversee rail services across England.

John Whitehurst, chief executive of GTR, said passenger feedback had played a key role in shaping the plans.

"Our customers told us that comfort matters, which was why we'd been working on plans to improve seating on Thameslink services," he said.

Thameslink operates services across the South East, including Sussex, Surrey and some areas of Kent.

articles.title: In 1945, brothers Alfred and Andrew Collier donated 146 Oregon acres to the state as a memorial to their parents; today, Collier Memorial State Park spans 536 acres and preserves the regionâs logging history
articles.summary: US News: Explore the rich history of Collier Memorial State Park, a tribute to the Collier brothers' parents, showcasing over 150 years of logging heritage and serving 350,000 annual visitors in Oregon.
articles.body: In 1945, brothers Alfred D. and Andrew Collier of Klamath Falls donated 146 acres of what would become Collier Memorial State Park to the state of Oregon as a memorial to their parents, Charles Morse Collier and Janet McCormack Collier. The initial 146 acres were only the beginning: over the next four decades, Oregon slowly acquired additional land, thus expanding the park to its present 536 acres. Today, the Oregon Parks and Recreation Department says that the park serves more than 350,000 visitors every year, combining outdoor recreation with one of the countryâs notable collections of historic logging equipment.A family memorial turns into a state parkThe Collier familyâs connection with the property went beyond the memorial donation. The brothers, Alfred D. and Andrew Collier, were involved with Klamath Falls business interests, including the Swan Lake Moulding Company, and their ventures left them with a significant collection of antique logging and lumbering equipment. According to Oregon State Parks, the idea of a logging museum was conceived by the brothers from the beginning, making the preservation of the regionâs timber history part of the parkâs purpose from its early years.In 1947, the brothers donated the first machines that would eventually become part of the Collier Logging Museum. Notably, the collection did not stay limited to those original pieces: donations continued over subsequent decades, while Alfred Collier reportedly continued finding new equipment for the museum until his death in 1988. Through these continuous acquisitions, the collection grew to encompass nearly 150 years of industrial timber history, chronicling the evolution of logging technology from the late 19th century onward.While the outdoor logging museum currently covers an expansive 146-acre footprint, matching the exact total acreage of the brothers' initial 1945 deed, the surrounding park footprint did not remain static. Instead, the state strategically acquired adjacent timber tracts over the years, absorbing the museum into a much larger 536-acre recreational ecosystem.The parkâs expansion from 146 acres to 536 acresThe park expanded over decades rather than in a single acquisition, with the Collier brothers helping acquire additional land through 1962, according to Oregon State Parks. In 1981, the final tract was obtained from the US Forest Service, completing the major additions that brought the park to its current size.Furthermore, the parkâs location helped shape what it became, with the Williamson River and Spring Creek converging within the property and the surrounding landscape connecting the park with broader forests and recreational areas of south-central Oregon. The Williamson River is regionally known for its trout fishery, while Spring Creek is a clear spring-fed stream flowing through the park. Today, visitors can camp, fish, explore trails and visit the outdoor logging museum.Meanwhile, the logging museum remains the parkâs defining historical feature, and its outdoor collection includes rare and antique equipment dating to the 1880s, alongside machinery from later periods. The exhibit underscores how timber harvesting changed as railroads, engines and mechanised equipment transformed the industry. Additionally, the museum contains a cabin village made up of buildings constructed between 1880 and 1920, which were originally sourced from a 100-mile radius across the pine-forested high plains of south-central and eastern Oregon and relocated to the park grounds.Transformation from private tribute to major public destinationThe state organisation reported that donations for the museum continued to grow long after the brothersâ initial contributions. They noted that donations for the museum continued to grow long after the brothersâ initial contributions, rolling in over nearly eight decades to establish a highly comprehensive regional archive.The park itself survived several changes that significantly affected its historic landscape, including the Two Four Two wildfire in September 2020 that burned through part of Collier Memorial State Park and damaged portions of the logging museum. The stateâs Park and Recreation agency reported that most of the museumâs roughly 10,000 artefacts survived, although two major pieces of historic equipment, one of its buildings and areas of the surrounding ponderosa-pine forest were damaged. Despite those changes, the original purpose of the property remains visible through the state-initiated intensive multi-year ecological restoration projects, hazardous tree mitigation, and historical structure rebuilds following the disaster. Thanks to these comprehensive recovery efforts, the park successfully reopened its gates in phases.Today, the parcel given to the state as a family memorial has become a public park that attracts hundreds of thousands of visitors annually, according to the state brochure. Within it, the museum preserves the history of the stateâs logging industry, while Williamson River, Spring Creek, the forest and the campground support recreation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal flash flood kills eight; damages roads, power projects
articles.summary: cNepal sent helicopters to the rescue on Wednesday after a massive flash flood swept away villages in the Himalayan nation, killing eight and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.
articles.body: Nepal sent helicopters to the rescue on Wednesday after a massive flash flood swept away villages in the Himalayan nation, killing eight and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said. Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with some missing in the neighbouring county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a land crossing between China and Nepal, the Xinhua official news agency said. The waters were too high for helicopters to land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, officials said, while flagging the risk of casualties. “There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” district administrator Narendra Pariyar told Reuters. “But I cannot say for sure now.” Pariyar urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi river in the area to seek higher ground, pointing to reports that nearby villages and infrastructure project sites were washed away. “It all came suddenly,” the Onlinekhabar portal quoted a witness from the area as saying. “We heard a loud sound, like a volcano erupting. People started to scream and ran away.” Nepal’s rescue helicopters would be unable to land in the affected areas until the waters recede, however, army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said. The cause of the inundation was not immediately clear, but a deadly flash flood on the same river last year was eventually traced to the draining of a glacier lake. China says Gyirong port affected The mudslide on the Nepali side hit China’s Gyirong port, Xinhua added, cutting off roads, communications and power in the Shigatse region near the border with Nepal, it added, without giving details. President Xi Jinping urged “all-out” search efforts for the missing as well as stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters. Nepal’s energy ministry said 430 MW of electricity supplies were affected, mostly from hydroelectric projects, or more than 12% of total national hydropower capacity of 3.2 GW, a Reuters calculation showed. Prime Minister Balendra Shah said police and military were joining rescue and relief teams. “Instructions have been given … to move the people living in the lower areas to safer places,” he said. “People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert.” From its origins in Tibet, the Bhote Koshi river empties into Nepal’s Trishuli river that eventually flows into India as the Gandak river. Last year’s Bhote Koshi flood killed nine people, with 24 missing, as it washed away a ‘Friendship Bridge’ linking Nepal and China to disrupt trade and transport for months. That flood was triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.

articles.title: In 1968, the Netherlands reclaimed land from the sea for factories; when the development was abandoned, birds colonised it and the accidental wetland became a 56-square-kilometre nature reserve
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the transformation of a 1968 abandoned industrial site into the thriving Oostvaardersplassen nature reserve, showcasing how ecological recovery can reshape landscapes and support biodiversity.
articles.body: In 1968, Dutch engineers drained a stretch of the IJsselmeer near Lelystad to create new land meant for factories and warehouses, a history recorded on the official site page kept by Nationaal Park Nieuw Land. The industrial estate was never built. The abandoned ground filled with rainwater and seepage, wild geese settled on it within a few seasons, and the site gradually became the Oostvaardersplassen, a wetland that now covers 56 square kilometres and draws researchers from across Europe.Part of a much larger Dutch programme to reclaim land from the old Zuiderzee for farms, housing and industry, the reserve lies within the Zuidelijk Flevoland polder. Planners expected the newly drained ground near Lelystad to carry factories once the clay soil had settled enough to build on. Workers sowed reeds across the marshy sections to stop that soil from shifting during the wait. The construction that was meant to follow never arrived, largely because the oil crisis of the 1970s slowed the wider Dutch economy and left the planned industrial estate on paper only. With no bulldozers on site, the reed beds and shallow pools simply carried on spreading through the wet clay. That gap between plan and outcome makes the Oostvaardersplassen unusual among nature reserves. Almost nowhere else in Europe did a protected wetland begin life as a rejected industrial park rather than a landscape someone set out to conserve.Geese arrived before officials changed their mindsGreylag geese found the marshy ground long before any government body decided what to do with it. Their grazing kept young willow and reed growth in check, which stopped the site from turning into scrubby woodland and instead let open water and reed beds spread further. That habitat pulled in a growing list of migratory birds, from spoonbills to great white egrets, along with species that had grown scarce elsewhere in the Netherlands.A group of ecologists led by Frans Vera noticed what was happening and began pushing for the site to be protected rather than eventually drained for the industry it was originally meant to hold. Their case succeeded. By 1983 the site had been formally designated a nature reserve by Staatsbosbeheer, the Dutch state forestry service, and in 1989 it earned recognition as a Wetland of International Importance, a status confirmed in the site record kept by the Ramsar Sites Information Service and normally reserved for wetlands with long, well-documented ecological histories rather than ones barely two decades old.From accidental swamp to a rewilding case studyOnce protected, the Oostvaardersplassen became a live experiment rather than a conventional park. Vera and the management team introduced Heck cattle, Konik horses and red deer to graze alongside the geese, aiming to recreate the kind of open, herbivore-shaped landscape that may have covered parts of prehistoric Europe. Left largely without supplementary feeding, the herds bred, competed for food and thinned out in hard winters much as wild populations would. That management approach was the subject of an in-depth account carried by Ecos.That approach has not been free of controversy. Harsh winters have periodically killed large numbers of grazing animals, prompting public debate in the Netherlands over how much human intervention a wild reserve should allow. Independent panels have since pushed for more active management of herd numbers, and rules around supplementary feeding have shifted more than once in response.The site has also grown in size and status since its early years. It became part of Nieuw Land National Park when that park was established in 2018, joining neighbouring dune and marsh areas under a single protected designation. Visitors can now walk marked trails along the reserve's edges and watch herds of horses and cattle roam ground that was originally planned for warehouses and loading docks. What began as surplus polder, too wet and too unstable for the factories it was drained for, is today one of the most closely watched rewilding sites in Europe, offering scientists a rare long-term record of how quickly wild habitat can reclaim ground that humans once carved out of the sea for entirely different purposes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dog treat founder eats her own products, even packs them in her kids' lunches
articles.summary: In celebration of National Dog Day, Lord Jameson's founder says the MAHA movement should extend to pets with organic, whole-food treats free of artificial additives.
articles.body: It's National Dog Day, and one dog treat creator thinks dogs should be included in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative, which emphasizes whole, nutrient-dense foods. "We have never used anything artificial," Sarah Goldberger, New York-based founder and CEO of organic dog treat company Lord Jameson, told Fox News Digital.  "We've never used fake food coloring. We've never used fake flavoring. All of our bright, beautiful colors come from real fruits and vegetables." CHEAP, HEALTHY FOOD IS REJECTED BY MOST AMERICANS EVEN AS MAHA MOVEMENT PUSHES IT Since becoming an official federal initiative in February 2025, the MAHA Commission has promoted a greater focus on whole, nutrient-dense foods while calling for reductions in refined carbohydrates, added sugars and certain artificial additives. Goldberger believes those nutritional priorities will "translate into the pet space." "My hope is that as a brand, we can inspire other pet brands to make better choices to really impact the lives and the health and wellness of dogs," she said. Goldberger started Lord Jameson in 2019, inspired by her late dog, Jameson, after noticing what she described as a void in the market for healthier dog treats. HERE'S WHY DOGS DON'T NEED 'HUMAN FOOD,' SAYS VIRGINIA VETERINARIAN: 'NO REASON FOR IT' "Jameson had gone through a pretty serious medical issue, and the medication he was being given actually created toxicity in his body," Goldberger said.  Goldberger said she wanted to offer treats made with "completely clean ingredients, organic, gluten-free, no preservatives, no toxins, no artificial colors or flavors." "So we started working with a homeopathic vet, and we were reminded of the power of plant-based medicine. A lot of the formulas, especially in our wellness products, are meant to serve dogs during a time of needed healing with plant-based products, more herbs and botanicals." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS When she set out to create the brand, Goldberger said she surveyed more than 1,000 pet parents and found that many reported their dogs had allergies or sensitivities to various animal proteins, preservatives and food colorings. Goldberger said she wanted to offer treats made with "completely clean ingredients, organic, gluten-free, no preservatives, no toxins, no artificial colors or flavors." Despite not using preservatives, the treats have an 18-month shelf life, which Goldberger said is "very difficult to achieve in production" and is "another key selling point for us." Lord Jameson, Goldberger said, has "truly reimagined what dog treats can be and should be." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She said she eats the treats herself and even puts them in her children's lunchboxes. They've been a hit with pet owners for a variety of reasons, including what Goldberger described as their effect on dogs' digestive systems. "As a dog mom myself, I know the frustration when you go to the store, you buy food or a treat, you bring it home and all of a sudden they have diarrhea," she said.  "Because we're using whole-food ingredients and no preservatives, you're going to get a nice firm poop after they eat. It sounds funny to say, but this is something you'll see in a lot of our reviews." Goldberger also said the treats can be suitable for some dogs with colitis, diabetes or other specialized dietary needs. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Lord Jameson has since launched a line of "protein-inspired" flavors as part of its Love Puffs line, made with organic sorghum, a whole grain that contains protein and fiber. Another feature that sets Lord Jameson apart, Goldberger said, is that the brand is "completely vertically integrated," with its manufacturing operations, including its kitchen, warehouse and fulfillment center, based in Boulder, Colorado. "We've had no price increase for three or four years, no issues with any tariffs because everything is sourced primarily in North America," Goldberger said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lord Jameson treats are sold at 5,500 independent pet retailers in the United States, as well as at some grocery stores, and are available internationally in four countries. Kelly McGreal of Fox News Digital contributed to this report.

articles.title: Australia to hand-vaccinate 5,000 wild penguins against bird flu spreading across wildlife; the birdsâ nightly routine will make the daunting task possible
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Australia is launching a necessary effort to protect one of its most recognisable coastal birds from H5N1 bird flu. Wildlife teams are hand-vaccinatin.
articles.body: Australia is launching a necessary effort to protect one of its most recognisable coastal birds from H5N1 bird flu. Wildlife teams are hand-vaccinating thousands of wild little penguins. On Phillip Island, Victoria, authorities hope to protect a colony of about 5,000 birds by catching them as they return to their burrows after feeding at sea. The operation comes as concern grows over the virus spreading beyond birds. SBS News reported that a second seal in South Australia was suspected of having bird flu, just a day after the country confirmed its first mammal case. The vaccination campaign is being carried out at night and is designed around the penguinsâ remarkably predictable routine. For the tiny birds, that familiar evening journey could now offer the best chance of avoiding a potentially devastating outbreak during the dangerous season ahead.Ambitious target to hand-vaccinate 5,000 penguinsThe answer lies in the little penguinsâ daily routine. Unlike many wild animals, little penguins return to their burrows at roughly the same time each evening. After spending the day at sea hunting for food, they come ashore around sunset and follow familiar routes back towards their colonies. That predictable behaviour makes it possible for wildlife workers to intercept them. SBS News reported that teams have been working late into the night to improve the process. They initially worked along quieter penguin pathways to learn how to handle the birds efficiently before moving to the western end of the penguin parade, where larger numbers return. By the weekend, another 600 penguins had been vaccinated, bringing the number that had received a first dose at Phillip Island and St Kilda to about 1,000.The birds are caught as they return from their daily trips to sea. They are then vaccinated, microchipped and released back towards their burrows. The entire operation is carried out at night, when the penguins naturally gather. It is an extraordinary amount of work for such small animals. Yet their habits make the task considerably more practical than trying to vaccinate other free-ranging species.Why are Australian authorities vaccinating wild penguinsThe little penguin population on Phillip Island is facing a serious new threat from H5N1, a highly contagious form of bird flu. The island is home to around 40,000 little penguins, while the specific vaccination effort is focused on about 5,000 birds. As per âA-Z Animals,â Victoriaâs programme is intended to become the worldâs largest vaccination campaign targeting wild birds. Each penguin needs two separate doses, meaning the same birds have to be caught twice. Officials also plan to microchip the birds so they can identify which penguins have received their injections.The need for action has become more urgent after H5N1 was detected among little penguins. A-Z Animals reported that one penguin on Phillip Island had already died from the virus shortly before the vaccination programme began. The danger is not limited to the birds. SBS News notes that five suspected H5 bird flu cases were recorded in South Australia on 24 August, including a long-nosed fur seal at The Pages Conservation Park. The animal was being tested, with results expected in the following days. That came just one day after Australia confirmed its first mammal case of a long-nosed fur seal at Beachport, about 300 kilometres south of Adelaide. Authorities believed that the seal had contracted the virus from wild birds.Little penguins are perfect for this unique operationWildlife vaccination is extremely difficult because animals move freely and can be hard to locate repeatedly. Little penguins offer several advantages. According to A-Z Animals, penguins live in colonies, return to the same burrows each evening and cannot fly away. Their predictable movements mean workers have a realistic opportunity to catch the same birds more than once. Phillip Islandâs famous penguin parade also means the birds are accustomed to people being nearby. Hundreds of thousands of visitors come to the island each year to watch the penguins make their evening return. Their familiarity with humans can make it easier for wildlife teams to work quickly while causing less disruption. For the conservation teams, that behaviour could make the difference between a vaccination programme that sounds impossible and one that can actually be carried out.How serious could an H5N1 outbreak becomeThe potential consequences are significant because Phillip Island supports the world's largest little penguin colony. Australian government modelling from May 2025 estimated that a worst-case H5N1 outbreak could kill between 8,000 and 16,000 little penguins on Phillip Island alone. The modelling also suggested that if vaccination began only after the virus was already spreading through a colony, it could be too late to prevent major deaths. That means the current campaign is not being treated as a guaranteed solution. Instead, vaccination is being used as one way to reduce the potential impact of the virus. The programme also matters beyond wildlife conservation. The nightly penguin parade is a major attraction on Phillip Island, drawing visitors who come specifically to see the birds return to their burrows. One local tour operator said that around 40% of his business came from penguin tourism. Protecting the penguins therefore also helps protect an important part of the islandâs tourism economy.Possibility of bird flu spreading among Australian wildlifeThe suspected second seal case has added another layer of concern. According to SBS News, Environment Minister Murray Watt warned that transmission from birds to mammals was likely to occur and that Australia could eventually experience the large-scale deaths of birds and mammals seen overseas. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins also said that the federal government is investigating whether vaccines could be used for mammals. Trials using a cattle vaccine were underway in North America, although no suitable vaccine is commercially available yet for Australian mammals. Meanwhile, the penguin programme could become a model for protecting other vulnerable species. A-Z Animals reported that Victoria was already considering whether other at-risk birds in captivity could be included in future vaccination efforts. For now, the focus remains on the little penguins returning home each evening. Wildlife workers are turning that simple routine into an ambitious defence against one of the most serious wildlife diseases Australia has faced.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Scottish scholar and his American wife bought the remote island of Canna; 43 years later they gifted it, their home and their lifeâs work preserving Gaelic culture to the National Trust for Scotland
articles.summary: UK News: John Lorne Campbell and Margaret Fay Shaw had already spent years recording Gaelic songs, stories and traditions when they made the remote Isle of Can.
articles.body: John Lorne Campbell and Margaret Fay Shaw had already spent years recording Gaelic songs, stories and traditions when they made the remote Isle of Canna their home in 1938. The Scottish folklorists continued that work from the island for more than four decades before Campbell gifted Canna, their home, library, archives and sound recordings to the National Trust for Scotland.According to the Trust, Campbell was born in Argyll on October 1, 1906. The eldest son of Colonel Duncan Campbell of Inverneill and his American wife, Ethel Waterbury of New Jersey, he was educated at Cargilfield School in Edinburgh and Rugby. He later studied Rural Economy at St Johnâs College, Oxford, as well as Celtic under Professor John Fraser of Jesus College.His interest in Gaelic had started in childhood and grew during his time at Oxford. With the help of Fraser, who became his mentor, Campbell began working on a Gaelic anthology. His first published book, Highland Songs of the Forty-Five, appeared in 1933.That same year, his work took him to the Outer Hebrides. He arrived on Barra on August 4, 1933, to study crofting conditions and colloquial Gaelic. The visit became the beginning of a long effort to collect and preserve Gaelic songs, stories and linguistic records.From Barra to CannaOn Barra, Campbell became involved with local people and explored the Gaelic traditions of the Hebrides. He started with an Ediphone Recorder using wax cylinders and later moved to a Presto Disc Recorder. He obtained both in New York and used equipment that was considered state-of-the-art at the time.Campbell also travelled to eastern Canada, particularly Cape Breton, to study Gaelic traditions among the descendants of 18th- and 19th-century emigrants. He found that Gaelic oral traditions were still alive after more than 100 years of separation from Scotland.In 1937, while in Nova Scotia, he also recorded the history and traditions of the Micmac Indians, the Indigenous people of the Maritime Provinces. He described Cape Breton as 'a Highland Community where there are no lairds'.Campbellâs life took another major turn in 1938 when he bought the islands of Canna and Sanday. He and Margaret moved to Canna after spending three years living on Barra.Campbell had met Margaret Fay Shaw in South Uist in 1934, where she was collecting traditional Gaelic songs. Margaretâs musical talents and Campbellâs knowledge of words and language, built what became a major collection of Gaelic cultural material.The couple lived at Canna House, which had been built around 1863 by Donald Macneil, who owned the island at the time. The house and island were later sold to Greenock shipowner Robert Thom in 1881. His family remained there until his death in 1911, after which the island was eventually bought by Campbell.Canna House became both their home and a place where they continued their research. Campbell spent long hours in its library transcribing and archiving his Gaelic recordings and writing academic works. Margaret continued her own work through photography and film.The 1981 giftIn 1981, Campbell presented Canna to the National Trust for Scotland. The gift included Canna House, the island, his library, archives and sound recordings. Campbell and Margaret continued living there and devoted their time to cataloguing and publishing their research.The National Trust for Scotland says the collection inside Canna House is of international importance. It includes material covering Gaelic folk songs and tales, Celtic and Norse studies, philology, music, literature and Scottish history.The archives also preserve Margaretâs photographic collection of more than 6,000 images from the early 20th century in the Hebrides. Campbellâs work includes 1,700 sound recordings, his Hebridean Lepidoptera collection and the research writings collected by the couple over about 60 years.The house also retains their furnishings, artworks and personal belongings, giving a record of the life they built around their research.Their work continues Campbell died suddenly on April 25, 1996, while on holiday at Villa San Girolamo in Fiesole, Italy. He had asked to be buried where he died, and he was initially interred there. In 2006, his remains were reinterred on Canna, in the bluebell woods he had planted as a young man. Margaret died in 2004. Their work, however, remained connected to Canna House through the collections they had built and preserved there.Magda Sagarzazu, who had known the Campbells closely, continued Campbellâs work after his death. She had first come to Canna from the Basque Country in 1960, aged 11, with her sister and father. She spent much of her childhood on the island and developed a close bond with the Campbells, particularly John.After Campbell died, Magda lived with Margaret at Canna House and continued cataloguing and documenting his archive of papers and books until she retired in 2015.Today, Canna House is open for pre-booked guided tours. Visitors can see rooms including the library, where Campbell worked, and Margaret Fay Shawâs study, which contains examples of her work in photography and film. Her Graflex camera is also displayed there, while a projector shows film footage of everyday life on Canna and South Uist.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Next Atlantic storm to be named 'Dolly' in an uncanny 'coincidence'
articles.summary: US News: The death of country music icon Dolly Parton has created an unusual coincidence in the Atlantic: the next tropical storm to form there is set to be ca.
articles.body: The death of country music icon Dolly Parton has created an unusual coincidence in the Atlantic: the next tropical storm to form there is set to be called Dolly. The timing is striking, but the overlap is entirely coincidental.Dolly had been on the predetermined 2026 Atlantic storm list years before Parton’s death. It appears on a list maintained under procedures established by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and was never chosen as a tribute to the singer.Atlantic storm names are drawn from rotating lists that are reused every six years unless a name is later retired. The system is established in advance so storms can be identified quickly and consistently once they reach the required strength, the news agency Associated Press reported.A coincidence written into the hurricane list years agoUnlike names chosen for commemorative events, tropical cyclone names are fixed well before a hurricane season begins.For the Atlantic, the WMO maintains predetermined lists of names that are used sequentially as qualifying storms develop. The names alternate between male and female, and the lists generally return on a six-year cycle unless individual names are removed.The system also serves a practical purpose. Giving storms distinct names allows meteorologists, emergency agencies, broadcasters and the public to follow individual weather systems more easily, particularly when several are active at the same time.How a storm earns the name DollyBeing next on the list does not mean the name Dolly is guaranteed to be used.For a tropical or subtropical cyclone to receive a name, it must reach tropical-storm strength, with maximum sustained winds of at least 39 mph (63 kph).If the next qualifying Atlantic system reaches that threshold, forecasters would assign it the next unused name on the 2026 list — Dolly.The name is therefore tied to the predetermined sequence of storms during the season, not to events involving any person who happens to share it.The system that could put the name into useThe National Hurricane Center (NHC) is watching disturbed weather in the eastern tropical Atlantic, south of the Cabo Verde Islands, where conditions could support further development.The system would first need to become sufficiently organised to be classified as a tropical depression. Only if it subsequently strengthens to tropical-storm intensity would the name Dolly come into use.That outcome remains uncertain, but the name is next in line because the Atlantic has already used the first three names designated for 2026.Those were Arthur, Bertha and Cristobal. Arthur affected the US Gulf Coast in June, Bertha brought heavy rain to parts of Louisiana and Texas in July, and Cristobal became the season’s third named storm in August before weakening.Their progression leaves Dolly as the fourth available name on this year’s list.When storm names disappear for goodWhile Atlantic storm-name lists normally return every six years, some names never come back.Names associated with particularly deadly or destructive storms can be permanently retired from the rotating lists. The practice prevents names strongly associated with catastrophic events from being used again in future seasons.That happened after the 2025 season with Melissa, a Category 5 hurricane that caused extensive destruction across the Caribbean and killed more than 90 people.Melissa was formally retired in 2026. When that list returns in 2031, the replacement name will be Molly.The process illustrates how storm names can acquire powerful associations only after they are used. Dolly, by contrast, remains simply the next predetermined name waiting on the 2026 list.A quieter Atlantic season in 2026The potential emergence of Dolly comes during a hurricane season that NOAA says is now most likely to finish with below-normal activity.In its updated August outlook, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) placed the probability of a below-normal Atlantic season at 75%, up from 55% in its preseason assessment.NOAA now forecasts seven to 13 named storms for the full season, including two to six hurricanes and zero to two major hurricanes.El Niño is one factor behind that outlook. It tends to increase vertical wind shear over the Atlantic, making conditions less favourable for tropical systems to develop and strengthen.Whether the disturbance south of Cabo Verde develops far enough to become Tropical Storm Dolly is still an open question. The coincidence with Parton’s death may be remarkable, but the name itself was settled years before the events of this week.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1925, New Yorker Gayer Dominick bought Bulls Island as a private hunting preserve; 11 years later he gave it to Cape Romain refuge for seabirds and shorebirds
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating history of Bulls Island, from its purchase by banker Gayer Dominick in 1925 to its transformation into a vital national wildlife refuge, supporting over 290 bird species.
articles.body: For 229 years, ownership of Bulls Island, a wild barrier island off the coast of South Carolina that is now part of Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge, passed through 36 different private hands, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which records that the island had 36 private owners from 1696 to 1936. The island and surrounding refuge now support more than 290 recorded bird species, with FWS documentation listing over 293 bird species in Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge. Then a wealthy New York banker bought it, built a mansion on it, and eventually turned it over to the federal government for good, setting the stage for a major shorebird refuge on the East Coast.Dominick purchases Bull Island as its 36th private owner since 1696Gayer Dominick, a New York banker and stockbroker with a passion for hunting, purchased Bull Island in 1925, according to reporting by the Post and Courier. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service records that he bought the island with the specific intent of turning it into a private hunting preserve. The refugeâs own visitor records say Dominick was the islandâs 36th private owner and this part of the chain of ownership goes back to 1696. Over roughly 240 years, Bulls Island changed hands repeatedly before Dominick eventually transferred it to the federal government. By the time Dominick arrived, Bulls Island had already lived through centuries of use.Dominick builds a sky-blue mansion and strings electricity across the Island Dominick had a large house built on the island soon after buying it, a sprawling structure that came to be known as Dominick House. The Post and Courier reports that Dominick was wealthy enough to string electric wires from island to island to power his retreat, at a time when only about half of all Americans, urban and rural combined, had electricity at all, though the great majority of urban households were already electrified by the mid-1920s. He also paid to have heavy equipment shipped in by boat so roads could be cut through the island's maritime forest, a level of investment beyond what most of the island's previous owners had been able or willing to undertake. The house Dominick built still stands today and Discover South Carolina notes that it later operated for years as an inn catering to visiting fishermen, birders, and other nature enthusiasts before eventually being converted into housing for refuge staff and volunteers.Outside the dwelling, Dominick's ultimate goal was altering the island's habitat features for his hunting pursuits. It was Dominickâs efforts, specifically, his alterations to Bulls Islandâs existing water impoundments to attract more waterfowl, as noted by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, that ultimately created the ecological conditions that later made the island so valuable for bird conservation. As the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has noted, Dominick's hunting-driven renovations for wetland environments created unforeseen uses far surpassing his personal agenda.Dominick Conveys Bulls Island to the Fish and Wildlife Service in 1936 Eleven years later, Dominick sold his interests (the whole island, his family's shore house and hunting cabin) to the federal government, ceding Bulls Island in 1936. The 1936 transfer added Dominickâs entire property, making Bulls Island the southernmost barrier island in the refuge, to the Cape Romain Migratory Waterfowl Refuge, which had been established in 1932 and later renamed Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge.The refuge expands to support seabirds and shorebirds along the coastCape Romain has grown in scale since Dominick made his gift. The refuge now covers more than 66,000 acres of barrier islands, salt marshes and maritime forest along South Carolinaâs southeast coast. In 1975, Congress designated 29,000 acres of the refuge as a National Wilderness Area under the Wilderness Act and the next year the refuge was designated as a Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network Site of International Importance. Bulls Island remains a popular part of the refuge, offering sanctuary to some 290 different species of bird, along with the alligators, deer and black fox squirrels who live in the same maritime forest that Dominick once hacked roads through. Visitors can still see the tabby ruins of the island's old fort and the Sewee middens, reminders of the islandâs long history before Dominickâs eleven-year ownership.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The Bulgarian village that fears becoming an Iranian target
articles.summary: US Air Force refuelling planes caused anxiety in Bezmer. While their departure has brought relief, tensions persist.
articles.body:
Bezmer, Bulgaria – The news landed on Saturday, bringing relief to nearby villagers: two United States Air Force (USAF) refuelling aircraft had left Bulgaria’s Bezmer airbase.

“The USAF air tankers took off yesterday and left Bulgaria,” the country’s defence minister, Dimitar Stoyanov, announced, as President Iliana Yotova declared: “For now, this mission is over.”

list 1 of 2 NATO ‘prepared’ to defend allies amid report of Iranian strike plans

list 2 of 2 Why Iran is threatening Europe’s ‘strategically important’ southeast

The US Air Force said the Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, intended to aid Washington’s war on Iran, had left to support “other operational requirements”.

The village had spent weeks worrying that the aircraft could make their area in southeastern Bulgaria a target for Iranian attacks.

Tehran had urged Bulgaria against allowing its territory to be used for the US and Israel’s military operation against Iran. Later, citing unnamed Iranian sources, the Financial Times reported that in the event of Washington’s escalation in Iran, Iranian forces had “assessed striking US assets in southeastern European countries such as Bulgaria” after Sofia had approved the use of its Bezmer airbase for US refuelling aircraft.

“I pray to God that our village won’t be attacked,” a woman working at a local grocery shop, who requested anonymity, told Al Jazeera days before the tankers left. “We are scared, but nothing depends on us.”

Although the planes are gone, geopolitical tensions – as well as fears in Bezmer of being drawn into the US-Israel war on Iran once again – persist.

This week, Stoyanov told reporters that Iran had carried out an effective hybrid operation, aided by Bulgarian politicians in the opposition.

“Unfortunately, this hybrid operation will continue,” he predicted in comments understood to have been directed at the opposition. Stoyanov did not elaborate further.

In Bezmer, a village of about 1,000 people that sits beside the base, Bulgarian military aircraft have long been part of the landscape. Many residents work at the base, according to Rosen Rusev, the mayor, and the sound of aircraft overhead is routine.

But in late July, the Bulgarian government proposed – and Parliament approved – the deployment of as many as eight US Air Force Stratotankers and up to 250 personnel.

Within two days, residents of Bezmer and nearby villages had collected more than 3,000 signatures against the deployment and held peaceful protests.

They did not want their village to become part of the war on Iran.

Rusev said a buzzy atmosphere took hold of Bezmer on Friday, when residents realised the tankers had left.

“Now they feel their voice is finally heard,” he told Al Jazeera. “It happened just as they wanted.”

The government had moved to reassure residents. Stoyanov said military intelligence had identified no threat to national security, the US aircraft or other facilities in Bulgaria. A United Kingdom assessment requested by the government had reportedly judged the risk as extremely low.

But reassurances did little to calm everyone.

With temperatures soaring to about 30 degrees Celsius (86F), two friends, Dinka Todorova, 67, and Ganka Vlaeva, 78, sat in plastic chairs in the shade.

Both have children who work at the airbase.

“We shiver day after day and pray that the war doesn’t come here,” Vlaeva said. “We are the first target, and many people will die.”

“And children, too,” Todorova added quietly. “For the ambitions of the greedy.”

Vlaeva said she was disappointed with the government and lawmakers, accusing them of ignoring the villagers’ petition.

“They don’t want to hear the voice of the people who elected them,” she said.

Not everyone in Bezmer shared that concern.

Ivan, a 33-year-old who sat beside the village church with his electric bicycle nearby, said that “groundless panic” was spread “recklessly”.

“There’s no danger for the village,” he concluded.

He is more worried about the possibility of interceptor missiles, or “something coming from Russia across the Black Sea”.

As residents protested, Antoniya Ivanova, whose father is a serviceman at the base, hung a white sheet over an aerial photograph of Bezmer. Animated films were projected onto it for children “to wind down the accumulated stress”, she explained.

“We’re the most innocent in this whole situation,” she said. “We didn’t want those aeroplanes near our homes.”

Children filled the playground as the afternoon cooled.

“Maybe there is a chance of attacks, but I think the media exaggerates,” said Tsonka Moskova, a mother in the village. “Whatever is meant to happen will happen. Those above us decide – the government. They are to blame.”

A low-flying AS532 Cougar helicopter passed overhead. Nobody looked up. The residents are accustomed to Bulgarian military aircraft.

Rusev, the fourth-term independent mayor, spent days trying to navigate between the villagers’ fears and officials. The protests were not an attempt to bring down the government, he said.

“We just wanted adequate information about the potential threats if the planes remained stationed here and what the guarantees for our safety were,” he said.

Social media made the situation harder, he added.

In Facebook groups, officials and experts struggled to compete with thousands of comments, many speculative and panic-inducing.

Military police also patrolled the village and the area around the airbase, adding to a sense of fear for some, and a sense of safety for others.

While Bulgaria is in the range of some Iranian missiles, some analysts argue that Iran is unlikely to have the capacity – or genuine will – for successful missile attacks against Bulgaria or elsewhere in continental Europe.

On Monday, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that the tankers had not made a single flight “south from the airport”, but had travelled to fellow NATO member nations for training and exercises.

But also on Monday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Tehran reserved the right to counter “any action regarded as supporting US and Israeli military aggression” against it.

“We have no issue with the Bulgarian people,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said. “It was previously announced – and reports have also confirmed – that several refuelling aircraft have left Bulgarian territory.

“As many Bulgarian citizens and politicians themselves have acknowledged, this action is contrary to international law and amounts to support for the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”

Back in the village, a woman said she was not afraid of Iran’s threats.

She did not want to be named or photographed for this article.

“I am definitely not scared. God is keeping us safe,” she told Al Jazeera. “I lie down and sleep in peace, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety,” she said, reciting a line from the Bible.

articles.title: Massive flash flood hits Nepal-China border, hundreds missing and many feared dead
articles.summary: A huge flash flood has swept through villages in Nepal. Police say at least eight people have been killed but there are fears the toll will rise. Follow for news updates.
articles.body:
• Villages devastated: A huge flash flood has swept through villages in Nepal. Police say at least eight people have been killed but there are fears the toll will rise. Nepal’s tourism board says at least 400 travelers, including foreign nationals, are missing.

• Tibet hit: Tibet has also been impacted, with Chinese state media warning of “major casualties.” A mudslide also hit China’s Gyirong port, where Chinese leader Xi Jinping urged “all-out” search efforts.

• Rescue operation: Helicopters are searching the area but waters in some parts are too high for them to land. The cause of the flood is not yet clear but deadly floods last year were traced to the draining of a glacial lake.

The flash flood which has devastated settlements in northern Nepal was caused by an earthquake triggering a large landslide which blocked the Bhote Koshi river, according to Nepal’s foreign minister Shishir Khanal.

“An earthquake occurred at 8:37 a.m. today, and due to it, a large landslide occurred, blocking the river, which appears to have caused the flood,” Khanal said during a meeting at the House of Representatives.

The United States Geological Survey, which records earthquakes worldwide, registered a 4.4-magnitude earthquake in the region at the same time as the one referenced by Khanal.

A deadly flash flood in Nepal has caused widespread damage to multiple settlements in the north of the country, killing several people.

Elsewhere, Tibet, an autonomous region of China, has also been impacted, with Chinese state media warning of “major casualties.” It is feared the death toll will likely rise, with search and rescue efforts currently underway.

Catch up on the latest developments here:

Hundreds missing: Nearly 400 travelers, including hundreds of foreign nationals , have been reported missing following the massive flash flood in Nepal, the country’s tourism board has reported, citing an initial assessment. This includes foreign nationals from India, Australia, The Netherlands, South Africa, the UK and Malaysia.

Helicopters struggling: Rescue helicopters cannot land in the affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in northern Nepal until the waters recede, the country’s army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said, according to Reuters.

Police and military join rescue: Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said police and military are joining the rescue teams, Reuters reported. “People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert,” he said.

China’s Xi responds: Xi Jinping has ordered an all-out search and rescue effort to find those who are missing after a mudslide in Nepal caused “major casualties” in Tibet’s Gyirong county, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua. Relief teams in Tibet will receive supplies including tents, heating stoves, clothing and bedding, China’s state broadcaster said.

CNN’s Issy Ronald and Simone McCarthy contributed reporting.

Rescue operations are underway after a huge flash flood swept through villages in Nepal and Tibet earlier today, with fears mounting the death toll will rise.

Known as the “rooftop of the world,” the Himalayan region is prone to flash floods and landslides, with experts clear that extreme weather is becoming more frequent and intense as the human-caused climate crisis escalates.

Here are some of the biggest natural disasters in the region in recent years:

August 2025: A surge of flood water tore through a mountainous Himalayan village in northern India, leaving several people dead and dozens missing. Rescue efforts were also hampered by mudslides.

September 2024: Days of heavy monsoon rains in Nepal triggered widespread flooding and landslides across the nation, killing around 200 people and causing widespread destruction.

October 2023: More than 100 people went missing in India’s northeast after heavy rain caused a glacial lake to burst, leading to flash floods which ripped through the Himalayan state of Sikkim.

October 2021: Rains and heavy flooding killed at least 150 people in India and Nepal, causing landslides to occur, bridges and houses to collapse, and rivers to burst their banks.

September 2014: Massive flooding hit parts of the Pakistan-administered Kashmir region and across the plains of Punjab province, wreaking devastation and disaster. The flooding killed more than 400 people across India and Pakistan, and displaced tens of thousands more.

The flash flood that hit northern Nepal on Wednesday was likely caused by an avalanche from a glacier, according to an expert at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) in Kathmandu.

The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group told the Associated Press.

The flood on the Lhende Khola was “triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” Sanyal told the AP.

The Bhote Koshi river flows from China into Nepal, often through deep gorges, and ultimately, into the Ganges in India.

Last year flooding on the river killed nine people, with 24 missing, according to Reuters.

Nepal’s Rasuwa municipality rises from the Himalayan foothills up to the border with China, where peaks higher than 7,000 meters dominate the skyline. Scattered villages of mud brick or stone buildings dot the ridges and hills along with terraces planted with maize and barely.

Mountain passes or particularly dangerous spots along its winding roads are marked by Buddhist shrines and strings of prayer flags. It takes around 5-6 hours by jeep to reach the Nepali capital Kathmandu from the border with China.

The region is home to around 50,000 people. In the north, Langtang National Park is a popular destination for trekkers, and Gosaikunda, a sacred alpine lake more than 4,300 meters up, is a major pilgrimage site for Hindus. The region is also home to several hydropower projects that tap into its fast-flowing rivers.

The Bhote Koshi river flows from China into Nepal, often through deep gorges, and is popular with white-water rafters. It flows through Nepal and ultimately, into the Ganges in India.

Rasuwa was devastated by the 7.8-magnitude earthquake that hit Nepal in 2015, killing more than 9,000 people, including hundreds in Langtang National Park who were buried after a landslide wiped a one-popular trekking village off the map.

Timure – located on the Trishuli river and one of the settlements feared hard-hit by the flooding – is the last settlement on the road to China. A string of buildings lining the road before the huge, imposing gate that marks China. It is typically clustered with lines of lorries, waiting to cross into China to pick up cargoes of clothes, electronics and household items.

China has mobilized multiple agencies to respond to the disaster in Tibet, with Chinese state media citing top leadership as guiding the response just several hours after it occurred – a sign suggesting the potential severity of impact.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping was quoted by state news agency Xinhua around 3:30 p.m. Beijing local time as calling for search and rescue efforts, resettlement of affected people and attention to “secondary disasters.” Xi is typically cited issuing such statements during natural disasters and other incidents, but those statements may not come until after the initial moment of response.

State media also noted China’s Premier Li Qiang had issued instructions to central agencies, while Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing was dispatched to Tibet to guide rescue efforts in the region, Xinhua said.

Disaster relief and emergency response agencies were allocating 30,000 items of central disaster-relief supplies, including tents, heating stoves, clothing and bedding, folding beds and moisture-proof mats, to support relief efforts in Tibet, according to China’s state broadcaster CCTV.

China’s Ministry of Emergency Management and the state-backed China Energy Engineering Corporation, which operates in the region, deployed emergency responders under a joint response mechanism.

An initial team of 200 geological, engineering and emergency response personnel equipped with reconnaissance drones, 3D laser scanners, life detectors and rescue equipment were mobilized, CCTV said.

Rescue helicopters cannot land in the affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in northern Nepal until the waters recede, the country’s army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said, according to Reuters.

Separately, Nepal’s army posted a video on X of one helicopter hovering just above a muddy outcrop beside the raging floodwater, indicating that search and rescue efforts are underway in the mountainous Rasuwa region in northern Nepal. Other pictures show service members carrying the injured on stretchers into a helicopter and an off-road vehicle.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said police and military are joining the rescue teams, according to Reuters.

“Instructions have been given … to move the people living in the lower areas to safer places,” he said. “People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert.”

Nearly 400 travelers, including hundreds of foreign nationals, have been reported missing following the massive flash flood in Nepal, the country’s tourism board reported Wednesday, citing an initial assessment.

articles.title: ‘I wake up with nightmares’: Ex-hostage who dug his own grave describes cruelty of Hamas captivity
articles.summary: Evyatar David tells CNN about his years in captivity, how music has helped him through difficult times after his release, and his determination to ensure the world remembers what happened.
articles.body: One year ago, Evyatar David appeared in a Hamas propaganda video, weak and skeletal, gripping a shovel in a concrete tunnel and digging what he said was his own grave. This month, the former Israeli hostage smiled as he stood at his older brother Ilai’s wedding playing guitar with his sister as the couple exchanged vows. “They tried to ruin our [lives] and our families’ lives and eventually they didn’t manage to ruin everything,” said David. He pointed to the wedding of another hostage, Eliya Cohen, as the ultimate form of triumph over captivity. “It’s the biggest closure and a huge moment of victory,” he said. The 25-year-old was speaking to CNN in his first international media interview since his release nearly a year ago, and as any prospect of peace remains elusive. He spoke about the starvation he endured in captivity, how music has helped him through the difficult months that have followed his release – and of his determination to ensure the world doesn’t forget what he and his fellow hostages went through. David was 22 when he was abducted from the Nova music festival during the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel alongside his childhood friend, Guy Gilboa Dalal. Two other friends in their group were killed in the attack. David and Gilboa-Dalal were taken to Gaza, where they spent most of their underground captivity together. David was among the last 20 living Israeli hostages in Gaza, released on October 13, 2025, after 738 days in captivity as part of the US-brokered ceasefire deal. In the months after his return, David largely avoided public appearances and focused on his rehabilitation. Last month, ahead of his first interview with Israeli TV, he revealed on social media that he is struggling with PTSD and other psychological effects. “It can surprise me any time, one hour I can be fine and happy, and next I can remember something from captivity, and get flashbacks. I wake up at night with nightmares, and it affects me all day after that. It’s very unstable and random,” he told CNN. David described what he calls “extreme starvation” during his captivity, which worsened in the months before the August 2025 video was filmed. “The starvation – beyond the lack of food and physical feeling that you’re always hungry – is the mental feeling that you have nothing to eat, and you don’t know if you will have food in one hour, tomorrow, two days, you have no idea what is going to happen and maybe you are going to die from starvation,” he said. The deep hunger caused stress and conflict even between hostages, he added. David said he was selected to appear in the video after his captors compared his physical state to Gilboa-Dalal’s. Since he looked worse, he said, “they decided I would be the actor of the video.” “It’s all staged, but it relies on the truth – we didn’t eat for three months,” he said. “Everything I say and do there – they told me to do it. You can see my body, I could barely move, when I tried to dig the grave, just to hold the shovel was almost impossible, probably the hardest physical thing I ever did.” When he told his captors he had almost collapsed, he said they ignored him. “I could hear them laughing, eating cakes and drinking tea, like there is nobody walking next to them that looks like a skeleton,” he told CNN. The guards, he said, had access to food, air conditioning, and television. “They told us there is no food in Gaza, but we knew it’s not true ‘cos we always saw the terrorists – they were fat and had muscles. We knew they were lying and starving us.” It was not the first time Hamas had filmed him for propaganda. In February 2025, he and Gilboa-Dalal were brought to the staged release ceremony of two other hostages and filmed begging for their freedom. The video was released by Hamas in what hostage families described as psychological terror. What sustained him underground, he said, was the thought of his family waiting outside, and the idea that “no matter how bad our conditions were, it could always get worse, so you can always find good things,” he said. “When you feel at your lowest is the perfect time not to give up, because that’s the point that can break you. Once you understand that and don’t let it break you, you can find yourself in a better place. It doesn’t matter what you have been through – don’t give up when you feel you are going to break because this is where the turning point can be.” David said his recovery is “very complicated.” He described himself as a “regular person” before he was a hostage. “Now it’s very different. It still takes time to process all this,” he said, “I’m trying to understand how to do good rehab and help myself with this.” His family and friends have launched a crowdfunding campaign for his rehabilitation, as he said the state doesn’t provide enough help to the former hostages. “I hope the next government will do better, I don’t know who it’s going to be, but I trust they will do better.” Music, David said, plays a significant role in his recovery process. During his captivity, his siblings organized weekly jam sessions in his honor at Tel Aviv’s Hostages Square. It has become one of his main coping tools. “If I feel sad or upset, it’s one of the best things I can do if I want to run from my thoughts and feel calm and unstressed. I don’t know what I would do without music.” Talking about his captivity is also helpful, he said, and he and his older brother plan to travel to the United States next month for a series of public appearances. “It’s very important for us to keep our stories alive and that people understand and remember what we’ve been through,” he said. “The world needs to know what happened and can’t forget about it.” Correction: This story has been updated to clarify that Evyatar David is 25.

articles.body: The US does not intend to carry out further military strikes on Iran âfor now,â secretary of state Marco Rubio has informed the foreign ministers of several allied countries, Axios reported, citing American officials.Instead, the Trump administration plans to intensify pressure on Tehran through other measures, including Washingtonâs ongoing naval blockade of Iranian ports.âRubio conveyed Americaâs plan to avoid initiating new military strikes against Tehran âfor the time beingâ.
